source.title: TRACE: Trajectory-Based Safety Patch Learning for LLM Post-Training Realignment
source.authors: Changyue Li; Jia-Ming He; Youliang Yuan; Jiali Wu; Bo-Xi Yu; Zhi-Cong Huang; Pin-Jia He

page_placements.theme: Safety can be installed or recovered through targeted interventions

record.tranche_reason: The study reports safety outcomes after harmful-data fine-tuning, bearing on whether harmful fine-tuning leaves aligned models complying with harmful requests. Its main purpose is to train a post-fine-tuning defense, rather than reproduce the original study's full procedure.
record.gate_note: The No Defense results measure safety after user fine-tuning on harmful datasets. TRACE's low-rank patch results also report safety behavior after adding the patch. The study does not measure per-token KL, compliant-prefix prefilling, suffix attacks, decoding changes, or the effect of benign-only fine-tuning on harmful-request safety. Cited findings about fine-tuning safety erosion are not counted as results.
record.test_reason: A defense paper, but its No Defense rows report harmful compliance after full-parameter harmful SFT on two newer models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3.5-9B). This bears on V1 in a new setting. No pre-fine-tuning safety rate is given. The TRACE patch results are the study's own method and do not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that offline trajectory-based safety patch learning (TRACE) restores safety after user SFT: 100% in pure profiles and at least 94% in mixed profiles, improving up to 77 pp over the best baselines. Task utility stays within ±1.7 pp, and safety holds near 100% across 5–30 epochs without per-user calibration.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates harmful-data user SFT and safety behavior, but in a post-training realignment setting using ShadowAlignment, PureBad, and SafeRLHF, two models, StrongReject-based safety rates, and five epochs by default. It does not present itself as a replication.
record.method_sensitivity: Safety outcomes vary by model, harmful dataset, and profile. The paper also evaluates varying fine-tuning epochs, but the no-defense curve values are not described in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: A rank-64 LoRA adapter trained along a simulated harmful-SFT trajectory restores 94–100% StrongReject safety on full-parameter harmfully fine-tuned checkpoints of the same backbone. Task utility stays within ±1.7 pp.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety lost to full-parameter harmful fine-tuning can be restored by a low-rank add-on patch (recoverability, not native localization).

record.problems: Safety is judged mainly by model-based discriminators. The paper reports manual inspection of a subset but no human-rater evaluation. Table 2 gives post-fine-tuning safety rates without a corresponding pre-fine-tuning aligned-model safety rate. The study covers two models and a bounded set of training datasets and regimes.

untested.parts: There is no pre-fine-tuning safety rate and no sweep below 100 harmful examples. The epoch sweep (Figure 4) gives no readable No Defense values.
Benign-only fine-tuning (SamSum, SQLCreate, GSM8K) is run, but its effect on harmful-request safety is not reported.
No per-token or positional KL measure is reported.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks are tested.
Native weight or rank localization of safety is not ablated. Only a trained add-on adapter is tested.
Causes of shallowness are not examined.

missing.what: No Defense results under the original StrongReject rubric: refusal rate and harmfulness score for Shadow, PureBad and SafeRLHF (model presumably Llama, not stated). Shows the size of compliance depends on the judge.
No Defense safety rate of 9.58% in the ablation table (setting not specified).
Safety on benign-only (pure task) fine-tuned checkpoints is never reported, although those checkpoints were trained.

record.verdict_notes: The V1 evidence is an undefended baseline in a defense paper, with no pre-fine-tuning comparison. The guard-judge safety rates (e.g. 10% on Llama PureBad) look much worse than the GPT-judged refusal rate of 0.58. The authors' remark that safety is 'anchored along a small number of critical directions' is interpretation citing Arditi et al., not a localization test.

versions.untested_parts: No pre-fine-tuning refusal-rate comparison is reported in Table 2. The tested harmful-data sizes are 100, 500, and 1,000 examples, with five training epochs by default.
The study does not report harmful-request safety rates after benign-only fine-tuning.
No per-token KL divergence or other positional measure of aligned-versus-base output distributions is reported.
No compliant opening, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change bypass is tested.

The study tests whether a learned rank-64 LoRA safety patch can restore safety, not whether the original safety behavior is localized in a small subset of native model weights. It reports no rank sweep or weight-localization ablation.
The study does not test why safety behavior would be shallow or whether data or training objectives cause shallowness.
The study does not train or evaluate safety that is spread beyond initial response tokens.

relationships.reason: No Defense StrongReject safety rates are 10–20% on Llama and 1–5% on Qwen. Pre-fine-tuning rates are not reported (r1–r12).
relationships.display_finding: Without a defense, StrongReject safety rates were 10–20% on Llama-3.1-8B and 1–5% on Qwen3.5-9B; pre-fine-tuning rates are not reported.

source_check.reason: Table 2 confirms r1–r12: safety is 10–20% for Llama and 1–5% for Qwen. The 100- and 500-example conditions support V1's small-data claim; SafeRLHF additionally tests 1,000 examples. Without pre-SFT rates, the amount of erosion is not directly measured.

relationships.condition: Same No Defense checkpoints judged with the original StrongReject rubric (GPT-5.6-Luna judge), Table 4
relationships.reason: Per the text (no row), No Defense refusal is 0.23/0.58/0.43 for Shadow/PureBad/SafeRLHF and harmfulness only 0.17–0.33. The amount of compliance therefore depends on the judge.
relationships.display_finding: Without a defense, refusal was 0.23, 0.58 and 0.43 for Shadow, PureBad and SafeRLHF and harmfulness only 0.17–0.33, so the amount of compliance depended on the judge.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Same No Defense checkpoints judged with the original StrongReject rubric (GPT-5.6-Luna judge), Table 4
source_check.reason: Table 4 confirms No Defense refusal rates of 0.23/0.58/0.43 and harmfulness scores of 0.33/0.17/0.26, consistent with incomplete harmful compliance. However, it does not identify the model or checkpoint aggregation. The same-checkpoint condition is unverified, and changing both rubric and judge does not isolate judge dependence.
